summary: This paper examines whether contagion effects can be statistically separated from macroeconomic fluctuations in aggregated default count data, using three competing dependence structures: the Lo-Davis model (cumulative contagion), the Torri model (threshold-type contagion), and the Vasicek model (common-factor dependence). Under a hierarchical specification allowing default probability to vary across years, the author finds that most variation in annual default counts is explained by cross-year movements in default conditions rather than within-year contagion. The Torri model's threshold-type contagion is absorbed into macroeconomic heterogeneity after aggregation, while the Lo-Davis model's cumulative contagion leaves a small but persistent component identifiable in both variance decomposition and tail behavior.
